name: Ozolotepec Zapotec

new_statements.quote: As stated above, most words are one syllable roots. If a word is multi-syllabic, simply stated, stress falls on the root. Prefixes and clitics never receive primary stress. In compounds or phrases, the stress is usually on the last syllable: gɪl:ˈgiʔd ‘sandal’, ngɪt ˈfrɪt ‘roasted chicken’ (frit ‘fried’ Sp. frito). Vowels in unstressed roots or of suffixes move to a more central vowel space, are reduced phonetically to schwa [ə], and sometimes are deleted, making identification of the vowel phoneme difficult.
new_statements.citation: Leander, Anita J. 2008. Acoustic correlates of fortis/lenis in San Francisco Ozolotepec Zapotec. M.A. thesis, University of North Dakota, Grand Forks.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are mostly monosyllabic roots; in polymorphemic words primary stress is on the root syllable, never on prefixes or clitics; in compounds and phrases the stress is usually on the final (root) syllable. Unstressed root/suffix vowels centralize to schwa or delete. The language also has two lexical tones (L, H) plus an LH contour with low functional load (§2.4, pp. 37-40), and vowel length is conditioned partly by stress placement (p. 33).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described for words; secondary stress is marked only in the elicitation frame phrase (p. 50, ex. 25: 'ˌ marks secondary stress in the phrase').
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually' on the last syllable of compounds/phrases; no lexical exceptions listed. Loanword diphthongs reduce to the vowel with primary stress (p. 42).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root vs. affix/clitic) plus a compound/phrase-level statement; based on 'initial analysis' of elicited words and frames from six adult male speakers of San Francisco Ozolotepec.
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand stress statement found describes San Francisco Ozolotepec Zapotec (SFOZ). Ethnologue (zao entry: 'Most towns with Ozolotepec in the name included, but not San Francisco Ozolotepec'; ztg entry lists San Francisco Ozolotepec), SIL Mexico and Leander herself (pp. xiv fn.1, 1 fn.2: 'SFOZ and SCXZ.. given the same ISO 639-3 code ztg') all assign SFOZ to Xanaguía Zapotec [ztg] = Glottolog xana1235, and Beam de Azcona 2019 treats it as Cisyautepecan, not Miahuatec. Glottolog nevertheless files the companion Heise 2003 sketch of the same community under ozol1235 (and its 2009 reprint under xana1235), so the SFOZ literature is the only 'description' Glottolog knows for zao. Ozolotepec Zapotec proper (zao: San Marcial, San Gregorio, San Juan Ozolotepec, San Mateo Piñas; the 'Ozolotepec variety of Miahuatec' per Beam de Azcona) has no located phonology, grammar or dictionary; its only open text is the 2007 La Liga Bíblica NT, which carries no orthographic or accent note. Recommend entering the Leander statement under xana1235 (currently marked the named source could not be reached in our check) and leaving ozol1235 as no-first-hand-source unless the reviewer accepts Glottolog's attribution.

new_statements.quote: El miahuateco, como es común en las lenguas zapotecas y aun en el tronco otomangue, es una lengua tonal, esto quiere decir que los cambios en el registro vocal permiten distinguir una palabra de otra. Por ejemplo, en localidades de habla miahuateca como Santo Domingo de Morelos (Hernández 2014), el tono permite distinguir entre la palabra jál “mamey” y la palabra jàl “milpa”. [...] Además, como he mencionado líneas arriba, el miahuateco es una lengua tonal. Esta lengua distingue cuatro tonos: dos simples, /A, B/, y dos complejos, /BA, AB/. Esta lengua distingue también vocales simples y vocales laringizadas.
new_statements.translation: Miahuatec, as is usual in the Zapotec languages and indeed in the Otomanguean stock, is a tonal language, which means that changes in voice register distinguish one word from another. For example, in Miahuatec-speaking localities such as Santo Domingo de Morelos (Hernández 2014), tone distinguishes the word jál 'mamey' from jàl 'cornfield'. [...] Moreover, as mentioned above, Miahuatec is a tonal language. It distinguishes four tones: two simple, /H, L/ [A=alto, B=bajo], and two complex, /LH, HL/. It also distinguishes plain and laryngealized vowels.
new_statements.citation: Hernández Luna, Mario Ulises. 2017. Hacia una caracterización geolingüística del miahuateco. Cuadernos del Sur (INAH/CIESAS/UABJO, Oaxaca) año 22, núm. 43: 88-104.

new_statements.relation_note: Tonal language, four tones (A, B, BA, AB); laryngealized vs plain vowels; six vowels incl. /æ/; 18 consonants with fortis/lenis; nothing on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Miahuatec Zapotec (the language of which Ozolotepec is treated as a variety) is a lexical tone language with four tonemes - high, low, and the contours low-high and high-low - realised on the (mostly monosyllabic) root together with a plain/laryngealized vowel contrast; nothing is said about word stress in this article (the author's 2019 thesis gives root/final stress only for Santo Domingo de Morelos, Mixtepec and Yautepec).
new_statements.exceptions: none; consonant and tone realisations 'pueden variar en las distintas regiones' (p. 95: /g/ = [j]~[w], /θ/ = [x] on the coast; p. 92 mentions 'la variación tonal en miahuateco' as a topic for later work)
new_statements.identity_note: A language-level statement about 'el miahuateco' (Glottolog subfamily Miahuateco miah1237, which contains ozol1235); the author's 2019 thesis (already read) counts San Marcial Ozolotepec as Miahuatec and Beam de Azcona 2018 calls the Ozolotepec/'costa noreste' towns 'otra variante más del zapoteco miahuateco'. The tonal example is from Santo Domingo de Morelos (loxi1235) and the article's own six-town survey (incl. San Miguel Suchixtepec and San Sebastián Río Hondo, two towns INALI groups with the Ozolotepecs as 'zapoteco de la costa noreste') concerns /ts/ only. NOT based on Ozolotepec data; Ozolotepec itself appears only in the migration history (pp. 92-93, 102). | A group-level characterisation of Southern Zapotec (macrocoatecano, miahuatecano, cisyautepequeño, Tlacolulita). P. 645 (scanned, gutter-damaged) describes Miahuatec as spoken 'en varios pueblos de los distritos [de Miahuatlán y Po]chutla, extendiéndose desde Cuixtla y X[..].. [San Agus]tín Loxicha en el sur, y a Ozolotepec y S[..]', i.e. Ozolotepec is inside the group the statement covers; no Ozolotepec forms are cited. The prosodic remark is explicitly about 'el zapoteco sureño' and 'lenguas macrocoatecanas, mia[huateca]nas y cisyautepequeñas'.

new_statements.quote: Elisión de vocales átonas. Un rasgo importante en el zapoteco sureño, pero que no es único de la Sierra Sur, es la tendencia a raíces y palabras monosilábicas. [...] En el zapoteco sureño las [vocales] átonas se han perdido en la historia, aunque nuevas vocales [átonas s]urgen en préstamos del español, y en palabras compuestas. [Las n]uevas sílabas átonas difieren de las sílabas tónicas por su falta [de con]trastes tonales. [La] monosilabicidad es fuerte en lenguas macrocoatecanas, mia[huateca]nas y cisyautepequeñas.
new_statements.translation: Elision of unstressed vowels. An important feature of Southern Zapotec, though not unique to the Sierra Sur, is the tendency toward monosyllabic roots and words. [...] In Southern Zapotec the unstressed vowels have been lost historically, although new unstressed vowels arise in loans from Spanish and in compound words. The new unstressed syllables differ from the stressed syllables in their lack of tonal contrasts. Monosyllabicity is strong in the Macro-Coatecan, Miahuatecan and Cis-Yautepecan languages.
new_statements.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2014. Algunos rasgos lingüísticos del zapoteco sureño. In Rebeca Barriga Villanueva & Esther Herrera Zendejas (coords.), Lenguas, estructuras y hablantes: estudios en homenaje a Thomas C. Smith Stark, vol. 2, pp. 643-660. México: El Colegio de México. (Author's scan, image-only PDF, 10 spreads.)

new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.relation_note: Southern Zapotec words are monosyllabic (stressed) roots; unstressed vowels were lost historically; new unstressed syllables from loans/compounds lack tonal contrasts. Nothing specific to Ozolotepec.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Across Southern Zapotec (Miahuatecan included, hence presumably Ozolotepec): native words are monosyllabic tonic roots because historical unstressed vowels were deleted; where unstressed syllables exist today (Spanish loans, compounds) they carry no tonal contrast, i.e. lexical tone is licensed only on the stressed (root) syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabicity is a tendency, not absolute (Tlacolulita has exceptions such as mba'ako 'perro'); no variety-specific exceptions for Miahuatec/Ozolotepec.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default convention for all varieties listed (incl. zao): stress on the penultimate syllable of the root unless marked otherwise; the nine zao forms given (ben, ja, jiˀ, ju, ke, kelioˀ, nit, ɡuʃ, θib) carry no stress marks and are mostly monosyllabic roots.

new_statements.identity_note: Corpus = '18 textos orales provenientes de cuatro narradores originarios de San Bartolo Loxicha' (p. 14), i.e. the Loxicha Miahuatec variety (loxi1235 area), not Ozolotepec; the tone line is the cluster-level inventory repeated from Hernández & Herrera 2024 (Santo Domingo de Morelos sketch, already handled under loxi1235). Ozolotepec is not mentioned. | Row keyed to ISO 639-3 zao 'Ozolotepec' (identifier as in Ethnologue) = ozol1235. Group-level statement: a transcription convention stated once for all varieties in the compilation. [name in source: zao Ozolotepec; pages 3 (Introduction), 3-63 (tables; zao row in each)]

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among sources on stress, because neither listed work says anything about it. The only stress statement on record for this glottocode (Leander 2008 §2.6 p. 43, root stress, prefixes/clitics never primary, compounds/phrases usually final) comes from the same San Francisco Ozolotepec community that Heise/Córdova 2009 describes, and both authors state that SIL/Ethnologue code that community as ztg = Xanaguía Zapotec (Glottolog xana1235); Ethnologue's zao explicitly excludes San Francisco Ozolotepec. So the identity conflict is between Glottolog's filing (Heise under ozol1235; SIL's own PDF keyword 'zao') and the authors' own coding (ztg), not between stress descriptions. Heise/Córdova's Table 5 footnote (a tonal difference between two enclitic forms) is consistent with Leander's two-tone analysis.
